n1.text: An email says your account will be locked in 1 hour unless you reset your password.
n1.evidence:
From: it-support@c0mpany-help.example
Subject: URGENT: reset your password now
Link: http://company-login.reset-verify.example/login

choices.label: Click the link and reset the password
Inspect the sender domain and the link target
Forward it to your whole team to ask if they got it too

n2.text: The sender domain uses a zero instead of an 'o', the link goes to an unrelated site, and the 1-hour deadline is a pressure tactic.
n2.evidence:
Sender domain: c0mpany-help.example  (real domain: company.example)
Link target: reset-verify.example
Tone: urgent threat + deadline

choices.label: Reply to ask if it is real
Report it to the security team and delete it

end-compromised.text: The page was a fake login form and the attacker now has your credentials.

end-spread.text: Forwarding put the malicious link in front of more people, and one of them clicked it.

end-risky.text: Replying confirmed to the attacker that your address is active, so you will get more targeted emails.

end-safe.text: Reporting it lets the team warn others and block the sender. Always check the sender and the link before acting.

n1.text: Students report that the class website intranet.school.example will not load. Your job is to find out why.
n1.evidence:
Browser: "This site can't be reached"
Server IP (from inventory): 192.0.2.10
Last change: firewall update yesterday

choices.label: Reboot the server right away
Ping the server's IP address
Turn off the firewall to see if it helps

n2.text: The server answers the ping, so the machine is up and the network path works. The problem is higher up.
n2.evidence:
> ping 192.0.2.10
Reply from 192.0.2.10: time=3ms
Reply from 192.0.2.10: time=2ms
0% packet loss

choices.label: Check that the name resolves to the right IP (DNS)
Reboot the server anyway

n3.text: DNS returns the correct IP, so name resolution is fine. Next, check whether the web service port is reachable.

choices.label: Test the connection to port 443
Add the IP to every student's hosts file

n4.text: Port 443 times out from outside, but the web service is running and listening on the server. Something in between is blocking it.
n4.evidence:
> Test-NetConnection 192.0.2.10 -Port 443
TcpTestSucceeded : False

On the server: web service RUNNING, listening on 0.0.0.0:443

choices.label: Review yesterday's firewall change
Disable the firewall completely

n5.text: Yesterday's update removed the rule that allows HTTPS traffic to the server.
n5.evidence:
Firewall change log (yesterday):
- REMOVED  allow tcp any -> 192.0.2.10:443
+ ADDED    deny  tcp any -> 192.0.2.0/24:3306

choices.label: Restore only the port 443 allow rule and document the fix
Allow all ports to that server so it never happens again

end-wasted.text: The reboot took 10 minutes and changed nothing. Guessing wastes time: test each layer in order.

end-workaround.text: DNS was not the problem, so the hosts-file change did nothing, and it now has to be undone on every machine.

end-exposed.text: The site works again, but the server is now open to the whole internet. Fix the specific rule, not the whole firewall.

end-safe.text: Site restored with a minimal change. You isolated the problem in order: ping the IP, then DNS, then the port, then the firewall.

n1.text: You receive an automatic alert: someone signed in to your school account from a country you have never been to.
n1.evidence:
Security alert - new sign-in
Time: 03:12
Location: unknown country
IP: 203.0.113.45
Device: Linux / unknown browser

choices.label: Ignore it, it is probably a VPN glitch
Open your account's sign-in activity page directly
Click the "Wasn't me?" link in the alert email

n2.text: The sign-in was successful, and the session is still active. A new rule also forwards all your emails to an outside address.
n2.evidence:
Active sessions:
- Your laptop        (this device)
- Linux, 203.0.113.45 (active now)

Mail rules:
- NEW: forward all mail -> backup.inbox@mail.example

choices.label: Sign out all other sessions
Delete the forwarding rule only

n3.text: The attacker's session is closed. They still know your password, though, so they could sign in again.

choices.label: Reset your password to a new, unique one
Keep the password, the session is gone anyway

n4.text: Password changed. Last step: make sure a stolen password is not enough next time, and clean up what the attacker left behind.
n4.evidence:
Password: changed
MFA: OFF
Mail rules: forward all mail -> backup.inbox@mail.example

choices.label: Enable MFA and remove the forwarding rule
Skip MFA, it is annoying

end-compromised.text: The attacker kept access for days, read your emails and used your account to phish your classmates.

end-phished.text: Links in security alerts can be fake too. Go to the account page directly, not through the email.

end-partial.text: You fixed one symptom, but the attacker still has a way back in. Contain first, then clean up.

end-relogin.text: An hour later the attacker signed in again with the same password.

end-safe.text: Account secured. Correct order: sign out sessions, reset the password, enable MFA, then remove anything the attacker changed.

title: Open port found in a scan

n1.text: The weekly scan of the school's web server shows an extra open port reachable from the internet.
n1.evidence:
Scan of 198.51.100.20 (from outside)
PORT     STATE  SERVICE
22/tcp   open   ssh
80/tcp   open   http
443/tcp  open   https
3306/tcp open   mysql   <- new

choices.label: Close every port right now
Find out what is using port 3306
Ignore it, the database has a password

n2.text: Port 3306 is the MySQL database used by the website. The website runs on the same server.
n2.evidence:
Process on 3306: mysqld
Config: bind-address = 0.0.0.0  (all interfaces)
Connections in the last 7 days: only 127.0.0.1 (local)

choices.label: Confirm with the site's owner who needs database access
Stop the database service

n3.text: The owner confirms that only the website on the same server needs the database. Nobody connects from outside.
n3.evidence: Owner: "Only the web app talks to MySQL, locally. No outside access needed."

choices.label: Block 3306 from outside and bind MySQL to localhost
Block 22, 80 and 443 too, just in case

n4.text: The change is applied. How do you know it really worked?
n4.evidence:
Firewall: + deny tcp any -> 198.51.100.20:3306
mysqld: bind-address = 127.0.0.1

choices.label: Rescan from outside and check that the website still works
Assume it worked and close the ticket

end-outage.text: The website went down for everyone. Close only what is not needed, and check before changing rules.

end-breach.text: Bots guessed the weak database password within days and copied the student table.

end-unverified.text: A typo in the rule meant the port was still open. Without a rescan, nobody noticed.

end-safe.text: Port 3306 is closed from outside and the website still works. You reduced the attack surface without breaking anything.

title: USB drive found in the parking lot

n1.text: On your way into school, you find a USB drive on the ground in the parking lot.
n1.evidence:
Label on the drive: "SALARIES 2026 - CONFIDENTIAL"
Location: staff parking, near the entrance

choices.label: Plug it into your school computer to find the owner
Plug it into your personal laptop instead
Pick it up without plugging it in
Leave it where it is

n2.text: At your desk, a classmate says: "Just try it on the old spare PC, it isn't connected to anything."
n2.evidence: Spare PC: shares the school Wi-Fi, logged in with a teacher's account

choices.label: Plug it into the spare PC
Refuse and take it to the IT/security team

n3.text: The IT team thanks you and asks a few questions.
n3.evidence: IT: "Where and when did you find it? Did anyone plug it in?"

choices.label: Give the place and time, and confirm nobody plugged it in
Drop it on their desk and leave

end-compromised.text: The drive pretended to be a keyboard and ran commands in seconds. The attacker now has access to the school network.

end-compromised-home.text: Your personal laptop is infected, and the next time you sign in to your school account the attacker gets your password.

end-left.text: Ten minutes later a curious staff member picked it up and plugged it in. Reporting is better than ignoring.

end-incomplete.text: Without details, IT could not check the cameras or warn others about more drives in the parking lot.

end-safe.text: IT found two more drives nearby and warned all staff. A tempting label is a classic lure: do not plug it in, report it.

n1.text: You get a notification saying your email and password were found in a data breach of an online shop you used.
n1.evidence:
"Your credentials for shop.example were exposed in a data breach.
Click here to secure your account: http://secure-check.example"
You used the same password for your school email and your gaming account.

choices.label: Click the link in the notification
Check the breach yourself on the shop's official site
Ignore it, it is only a shopping account

n2.text: The shop confirms the breach. Since you reused the password, attackers can try it on your other accounts.
n2.evidence:
shop.example: "Passwords from our 2026 breach may be exposed."
Same password used on: shop.example, school email, gaming account

choices.label: Change the password on the shop only
Change it on every account that used it

n3.text: You need three new passwords. How do you pick them?

choices.label: Use one new strong password for all three
Generate a unique password for each one with a password manager
Write them on a sticky note on your screen

n4.text: Each account now has a unique password. One last protection is available.
n4.evidence:
Password manager: 3 entries saved
MFA on school email: OFF

choices.label: Turn on MFA, starting with your email account
Skip it, unique passwords are enough

end-phished.text: The "secure your account" page was a phishing site that collected your password again.

end-takeover.text: Attackers tried the leaked password on other sites (credential stuffing) and took over your school email.

end-reuse.text: As long as one password is shared between accounts, one leak can open all of them.

end-sticky.text: Anyone walking past your desk can read your passwords. Store them in a password manager.

end-partial.text: Better, but if a password leaks again nothing else protects your email, which can reset all your other accounts.

end-safe.text: Fully protected: changed everywhere, unique passwords from a manager, and MFA on your most important account.
